user: Coffee brand, comparing channels and email jumped out — conversion rate dropped 8% this week vs last week. That's on 112 conversions. I'm ready to overhaul the whole email strategy. Where do I start?
assistant:
Start by doing nothing. Seriously.

An 8% move in conversion rate on 112 conversions is noise, not a trend. At that sample size the week-to-week wobble from pure randomness is easily bigger than 8% — a handful of buyers landing on one side of the week instead of the other moves the number by that much. You're about to rebuild a strategy on top of a coin-flip.

This is the single most expensive habit a founder can have: reacting to one noisy week, changing things, then reacting to the next noisy week the change happened to coincide with, and whipsawing the account into the ground.

What would actually count as a signal: the same direction holding for 3-4 weeks in a row, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band on this volume. Until then, leave the email program exactly as it is and look at it again at month-end. If you're itching to act, spend that energy growing the sample — get the volume up so next month's numbers are actually readable.

user: Eyewear, YouTube, last 30 days. Why is my CTR low? 1.11M impressions, 15,806 clicks, CTR 1.4%. But only 142 orders — conversion rate 0.9%. AOV ₹2,100. I'm running broad-match keywords. Trying to get that CTR up.
assistant:
Your CTR isn't the problem — chasing it would make things worse. Look one step down the funnel.

1.4% CTR is perfectly normal; 15,806 clicks off 1.11M impressions is plenty of traffic. The number that matters is the 0.9% conversion rate. You're pulling clicks in volume but barely 1 in 100 buys. When CTR is fine and conversion is dead, you're not facing an ad problem — you're facing an intent problem.

The cause is sitting in your setup: broad-match keywords. Broad match casts wide and drags in people researching, comparing, window-shopping 'sunglasses', 'eyewear', 'best glasses' — browsing, not buying. They click because the ad is relevant to their search; they don't convert because they were never in buying mode. If anything, a higher CTR on broad match just means more low-intent clicks burning budget.

The lever is intent, not clicks. Tighten to high-intent, bottom-of-funnel keywords (buying language, brand and product-specific terms), pile on negative keywords to choke off the browse traffic, and stop optimising toward clicks — optimise toward purchases. You'll likely see CTR dip and orders rise, which is exactly the trade you want.

Caveat: 142 orders is a usable but not huge sample, so make the keyword shift and give it a couple of weeks before judging the new conversion rate — and check the search-terms report to see exactly which broad queries are bleeding you.
